california: California covers 163,696 square miles and is bordered by Oregon to the north, Nevada to the east, Arizona to the south-east, the Mexican state of Baja California to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. In the middle lies the Central Valley, bounded by the Sierra Nevada and the coastal ranges, the state's agricultural heartland. The name most likely comes from the mythical island of California in the 1510 romance The Adventures of Esplandián by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo, whose Queen Calafia ruled a remote land rich in gold and pearls. The name was on a map by 1541. The Spaniards called the peninsula of Baja California Las Californias, and the name spread north to Alta California.

Before European colonisation California was one of the most culturally and linguistically diverse areas of pre-Columbian North America. Historians generally agree that at least 300,000 people lived there, in more than 70 ethnic groups. They managed their environments in complex ways, with forest gardening and controlled burning to prevent destructive wildfires, and political organisation ranged from bands and villages to large chiefdoms on the rich coasts, among them the Chumash, Pomo and Salinan.

European exploration in the 16th and 17th centuries led to colonisation by the Spanish Empire. The area became part of Mexico in 1821. In the Mexican-American War the United States conquered California, and Mexico ceded it in 1848. The gold rush that began that year brought social and demographic changes, among them what has been called the California genocide of the Indigenous peoples. California was admitted as the 31st state in 1850, as a free state, following the Compromise of 1850.

Sacramento is the state capital, and Los Angeles is its most populous city. California is the most populous US state, with over 39 million people. Hollywood has been an important centre of the film industry since the 1920s, and Silicon Valley in the San Francisco Bay Area is a centre of the technology industry.
cambodia: Cambodia covers about 181,035 km2 and lies entirely within the tropics, with a 443 km coastline along the Gulf of Thailand. Its landscape is a low-lying central plain surrounded by uplands and low mountains, including the Tonle Sap, the Great Lake, and the upper Mekong delta. The Tonle Sap's most distinctive feature is its flooding, from about 2,590 km2 in the dry season to about 24,605 km2 in the rainy season, and the plain around it, devoted to wet rice cultivation, is the heartland of the country.
The highest peak is Phnom Aural, at 1,813 metres. The Khmer name derives from the Sanskrit Kambujadeśa, the land of the sons of Kambu, after a sage from whom the Khmer kings claimed descent.

Cambodia has been inhabited for over 5000 years. The cave of Laang Spean, with radiocarbon dates around 6000 BCE, is considered the most ancient archaeological site in the country, and the first rice farmers came from the north from the third millennium BCE. Iron was worked by about 500 BCE. In the 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries the Indianised kingdoms of Funan and its successor Chenla coalesced in what became Cambodia and southwestern Vietnam, and for more than 2,000 years the region absorbed influences from India and passed them to other Southeast Asian civilisations.

In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself king, uniting the warring Khmer princes of Chenla under the name Kambuja, and the Khmer Empire became the centre of power. Over 600 years it facilitated the spread of first Hinduism and then Buddhism across Southeast Asia. In the 15th century Cambodia declined and lost territory to its neighbours, and during the Post-Angkor period Vietnam and Thailand each attempted to vassalise it. It became a French protectorate in 1863 and secured independence in 1953.

The Khmer Rouge regime carried out the Cambodian genocide from 1975 to 1979 and was deposed by a Vietnamese intervention and occupation, though insurgencies continued until 1999. By 1993 a United Nations peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and established a democratic constitution with elections. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy. About 17 million people live there, 95.8% of them ethnic Khmer.
camel: The camel is an even-toed ungulate of the genus Camelus, marked by fatty deposits known as humps. Three species survive. The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world's camel population and the two-humped Bactrian camel 6%. The wild Bactrian is a distinct species, not the ancestor of the domestic Bactrian. Camels provide milk, meat, fibre and felt, and are a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.

The hump is a reservoir of fatty tissue, a reserve of calories and not of water, as is commonly believed. A dromedary can drink as seldom as once every 10 days even in great heat, and can lose up to 30% of its body mass through dehydration.

Camelids originated in North America during the Eocene. Paracamelus, the ancestor of modern camels, crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late Miocene, around 6 million years ago. The camels that stayed in North America were wiped out 10 to 12,000 years ago, when the first indigenous peoples spread there from Asia, although fossils have never been associated with definitive evidence of hunting.

When humans first domesticated camels is disputed. Dromedaries may have been domesticated in Somalia or South Arabia in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the Bactrian in central Asia around 2,500 BCE, as at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran. A study of 2016 using mitochondrial DNA suggested that the dromedary was first domesticated in the southeast Arabian Peninsula.

Excavations in the Timna Valley in 2009 to 2013, led by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, found what may be the earliest domestic camel bones in Israel or outside the Arabian Peninsula, dating to around 930 BCE. The find drew attention because camels appear in the biblical stories of Abraham, Jacob, Esau and Joseph, and it is taken as strong evidence that those stories were written after that time. The archaeologist William F. Albright had earlier seen the camels of the Bible as an anachronism.

Camels introduced to Australia as transport animals in the 19th and early 20th centuries became a large feral population. The United States Camel Corps experiment of the 19th century also brought camels to the Southwestern United States.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonization, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
canary-islands: The Canary Islands are an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 100 kilometres off the northwest coast of Africa. The seven main islands, from largest to smallest by area, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. All are volcanic in origin, and with the Azores, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Savage Isles they form the Macaronesia ecoregion. Historically the chain was called the Fortunate Isles.

The western islands, El Hierro, La Palma and La Gomera, are influenced by the moist Canary Current and carry extensive subtropical laurisilva forest, while Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, nearest to Africa, are effectively desert or semi-desert. Mount Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain.

Linguistic, genetic and archaeological analyses indicate that indigenous peoples were living on the islands at least 2,000 years ago, possibly 3,000, and shared a common origin with the Amazighs of the nearby North African coast. They may have reached the islands in several small boats, landing first on Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. They came to be known collectively as the Guanches, although that name had belonged only to the indigenous inhabitants of Tenerife.

According to a 2024 study by the University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, archaeological evidence shows that the Romans were the first to establish contact, between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. During the Age of Sail the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons on the way to the Americas, which sailed that far south to catch the prevailing northeasterly trade winds.

The archipelago is the southernmost autonomous community of Spain, established in 1982. It has two provinces, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas, created by splitting the Province of Canary Islands in 1927, and the cities of Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria are joint capitals.

The name Islas Canarias probably derives from the Latin Canariae Insulae, meaning Islands of the Dogs, from Pliny the Elder's account of vast multitudes of very large dogs on Canaria. The canary bird takes its name from the islands. San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife is a World Heritage Site, as is Mount Teide.
canberra: Canberra lies near the Brindabella Ranges, part of the Australian Alps, about 150 km inland from Australia's east coast. Its urban area has an elevation of about 580 m, and the highest point near it is Mount Majura at 888 m. The Molonglo River was dammed to form Lake Burley Griffin, and it then flows into the Murrumbidgee. The area was a flood plain before the lake was filled.

The name derives from the Ngunnawal language of a local clan that the first British colonists called the Canberry, Kanberri or Nganbra tribe. Joshua John Moore, the first European landowner in the region, named his grant Canberry in 1823. The form Canberra began to appear around 1857. Suggested meanings include meeting place.

The first peoples of the area include the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. Archaeological evidence suggests human activity there 21,000 years ago. The Canberry or Nganbra clan lived mostly around Sullivan's Creek and had ceremonial grounds at the base of Galambary (Black Mountain), while the Pialligo clan had land around what is now Canberra Airport. The people managed the land with fire, farmed yams and hunted. Galambary was a meeting and business site, mainly for men, and an initiation site.

European settlement began in the first half of the 19th century. The federation of the Australian colonies was achieved on 1 January 1901, and the new capital was founded and formally named Canberra in 1913, as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne. It is an entirely planned city, based on a design by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, influenced by the garden city movement and aligned with landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie and Capital Hill.

Canberra is the capital of Australia and the largest population centre in the Australian Capital Territory, with an estimated 484,630 people. It is the country's largest inland city. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House, Government House and the High Court, and it hosts all foreign embassies in Australia.

Among its national institutions are the Australian War Memorial, the Australian National University, established in 1946, the National Gallery, the National Museum and the National Library. The Royal Military College Duntroon is also there, and Floriade is the largest flower festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
cape-town: Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, at a latitude of about 33.55 degrees south. Table Mountain, with near vertical cliffs and a flat summit more than 1,000 metres high, forms a mountainous backdrop with Devil's Peak and Lion's Head on either side and creates the City Bowl, which holds the central business district. To the south the Cape Peninsula runs 40 kilometres into the Atlantic Ocean and ends at Cape Point, and many suburbs lie on the Cape Flats, a plain that joins the peninsula to the mainland. Robben Island in Table Bay is part of the city, and Table Mountain National Park lies within its boundaries.

The earliest known remains of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin have since been revised to the mid-Holocene. Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to reach the area, arrived in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because the opening of a sea route to India raised such optimism, and Vasco da Gama recorded sighting it in 1497. In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed by the Khoikhoi Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Ships of several nations, mainly Portuguese, regularly stopped in Table Bay in the late sixteenth century on the way to the Indies. They traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans of the region for fresh meat and other provisions. In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the United East India Company were sent to establish a way-station for ships travelling to the Dutch East Indies, and they built the Fort de Goede Hoop, later replaced by the Castle of Good Hope.

The settlement grew slowly because adequate labour was hard to find. The shortage led the local authorities to import enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar, many of whom are ancestors of the present Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape. It is the country's oldest city. It has the highest density of Cape Dutch buildings in the world, a style that combines the architectural traditions of the Netherlands, Germany, France and Indonesia. Mostert's Mill in Mowbray, built in 1796, is the only complete windmill in South Africa. The Cape Floristic Region, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444. The islands are divided into the Barlavento or windward group in the north and the Sotavento or leeward group in the south. Santiago is the largest and holds the capital, Praia.

The islands were uninhabited before the arrival of Europeans. Genoese and Portuguese navigators found them around 1456. Portuguese records credit the first discoveries to António de Noli, born in Genoa, who was later appointed governor by King Afonso V. In 1462 Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande on Santiago, today called Cidade Velha, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics.

In the 16th century the islands prospered from the Atlantic slave trade. The English privateer Francis Drake sacked Ribeira Grande twice in 1585, when it was part of the Iberian Union, and after a French attack in 1712 the town declined relative to Praia, which became the capital in 1770. The decline of the slave trade in the 19th century brought economic crisis, but the islands' position on mid-Atlantic shipping lanes made them a good place to resupply ships, and the harbour of Mindelo grew into a commercial centre. In 1951 Portugal changed the status of Cape Verde from a colony to an overseas province in an attempt to blunt nationalism. The country became independent in 1975.

Cape Verde is a unitary semi-presidential republic whose constitution was adopted in 1980 and revised in 1992, 1995 and 1999. Praia is the capital and largest city. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole, called Kriolu, is the mother tongue of virtually all Cape Verdeans. The people descend from Africans, free or enslaved, and Europeans of various origins, and the diaspora outnumbers the people on the islands.
capitalism: Capitalism in its modern form is traced to agrarian capitalism and mercantilism in the early Renaissance, in city-states such as Florence. Capital had existed on a small scale for centuries in merchant, renting and lending activities. During the Islamic Golden Age, Arabs promulgated policies such as free trade and banking, and their use of Indo-Arabic numerals facilitated bookkeeping; these innovations reached Europe through Venice and Pisa.

In 16th-century England the manorial system broke down, land became concentrated in fewer landlords and workers were increasingly employed in a money-based economy instead of as serfs. From the 16th to the 18th centuries mercantilism prevailed, a system of trade for profit, though goods were still largely produced by non-capitalist methods. Most scholars see it as the origin of the modern system, but Karl Polanyi held that capitalism required generalised markets for land, labour and money, and so could not be said to exist before 1834, when a competitive labour market was established in England.

Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit. Its elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets and wage labour. Its forms, among them laissez-faire, state and welfare capitalism, differ in their degree of free markets, public ownership and regulation. There is no universally agreed definition.

The term capitalist, meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. Louis Blanc in 1850 and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in 1861 are credited with the first modern use of capitalism, and Karl Marx wrote of the capitalist mode of production in Das Kapital (1867). Because socialist critics coined the word, Robert Hessen called it a term of disparagement.

The Industrial Revolution of the 18th century made capitalism the dominant mode of production, characterised by factory work and a complex division of labour. It spread across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the 19th century it was largely unregulated; after World War II it became more regulated through Keynesianism, followed from the 1980s by a return of less regulated capitalism termed neoliberalism.
caracas: Caracas lies along the Guaire River in the Caracas Valley of the Venezuelan Central Range, a small and irregular valley close to the Caribbean Sea. A steep range, Cerro El Ávila, rises 2,200 metres between the valley and the shore, and about 15 kilometres of El Ávila National Park separate the city from the coast. The valley floor lies between 870 and 1,043 metres above sea level, and the historic centre stands at about 900 metres. The highest point of the Capital District, Pico El Ávila, reaches 2,159 metres.

The Guaire crosses the city and empties into the Tuy River. The city is occasionally struck by earthquakes, notably in 1641, 1812 and 1967. The region was formed in the Late Cretaceous, and the city sits mostly on metamorphic rock.

Before the city was founded in 1567, the valley was populated by indigenous peoples. Francisco Fajardo, the son of a Spanish captain and a Waikeri cacique, began establishing settlements around La Guaira and the Caracas valley between 1555 and 1560. His plantation of 1562 did not last, as natives of the region led by Terepaima and Guaicaipuro destroyed it, as they had destroyed the Villa de San Francisco founded by Juan Rodríguez de Suárez in 1561.

The settlers who eventually founded Caracas came from Coro, the capital of the German colony of Klein-Venedig, which Spaniards had controlled in practice from the 1540s. Moving eastward, they founded inland towns including Barquisimeto and Valencia before reaching the valley. In 1591 Simón de Bolívar, an ancestor of the liberator Simón Bolívar, petitioned King Philip II for a coat of arms. The king granted it by Royal Cedula on 4 September 1591 and declared Caracas The Most Noble and Very Loyal City of Santiago de León de Caracas.

Caracas is the capital and largest city of Venezuela and the centre of a metropolitan region estimated at over 5 million people. Its historic centre is the Caracas Cathedral on Bolívar Square. The Central University of Venezuela, founded in 1721, is the oldest university in the country, and its campus, designed by the architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

In the 1940s and 1950s, after the Second World War, a wave of European immigrants, mainly Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, settled in the country, and the city has been shaped by many ethnic and cultural groups. The Caracas Metro has operated since 27 March 1983.
carl-linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus was born on 23 May 1707 in the village of Råshult in Småland, Sweden, the first child of Nicolaus (Nils) Linnaeus and Christina Brodersonia. His father, a Lutheran minister and amateur botanist, taught him Latin as a small child, and the family moved to the rectory of Stenbrohult when his father became rector there. Linnaeus liked plants from his earliest years, and his father gave him his own patch of land to grow them.

In 1727, at the age of 21, he enrolled at Lund University. Most of his higher education was at Uppsala University, where he began giving lectures in botany in 1730. In May 1732 he set out on an expedition to Lapland, funded by a grant from the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala, curious about the Sami people.

In April 1735 Linnaeus travelled to the Dutch Republic to study medicine at the University of Harderwijk, and he published the first edition of his Systema Naturae in the Netherlands. After returning to Sweden on 28 June 1738 he worked as a physician at the Admiralty in Stockholm and helped found the Royal Swedish Academy of Science, becoming its first Praeses by drawing of lots. He later became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala, and in the 1740s he was sent on several journeys through Sweden to find and classify plants and animals.

He taught many students, 17 of whom he called his apostles, and they made botanical expeditions around the world, so that his system spread without his travelling outside Sweden again. He was ennobled in 1761. Illness troubled his last years, and he died on 10 January 1778 in Hammarby.

The first edition of Systema Naturae, printed in 1735, ran to twelve pages. By its 10th edition in 1758 it classified 4,400 species of animals and 7,700 species of plants. Linnaeus's main contribution to taxonomy was the establishment of universally accepted conventions for naming organisms, and his work marks the starting point of the consistent use of binomial nomenclature.

The Linnaean system placed nature in a nested hierarchy of three kingdoms divided into classes, orders, genera and species. His taxonomy of human races has been criticised in the 21st century: some regard him as a forebear of scientific racism, while others hold that his classification was stereotyped but did not imply that any race was superior.
caspian-sea: The Caspian Sea is an endorheic basin lying east of the Caucasus, west of the steppe of Central Asia, south of the plains of Southern Russia and north of the Iranian Plateau. It covers 371,000 square kilometres, stretches 1,200 kilometres from north to south with an average width of 320 kilometres, and lies about 27 metres below sea level. Its salinity is about a third of that of average seawater. The Volga, Europe's longest river, is its main freshwater inflow, entering at the shallow north end.

Like the Black Sea, it is a remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea, and it became landlocked in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level. The Caspian seal is the only aquatic mammal endemic to it, and the sea is known for its caviar and oil industries.

The earliest hominid remains found around the Caspian are from Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old, and finds in the Hotu and Kamarband caves in Iran suggest human habitation south of the sea as early as 11,000 years ago. The sea's name derives from the ancient Caspi people, who lived to its southwest. Strabo wrote that the territory called Caspiane was named after the Caspian tribe, as was the sea, but that the tribe had disappeared. Greeks and Persians in antiquity called it the Hyrcanian Sea.

Other names reflect later powers. Arabic writers called it the sea of the Khazars, and Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen still call it the Khazar sea after the Khazar Khaganate, a large empire based north of the sea between the 7th and 10th centuries. Since the medieval period traders reached it by portages linking the Volga with the Don and with rivers flowing into the Baltic, and canals followed from the early 18th century. Its shores were bordered in turn by Safavid, Afsharid, Zand, Qajar and Pahlavi Iran, and by the Tsardom of Russia, the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.

Five states border the sea along about 4,800 kilometres of coastline: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. A treaty of 1931 between Iran and the Soviet Union stated that the sea belonged to both. Whether it is in law a sea or a lake was long debated among the five, because the answer decides access to oil and natural gas, fishing and international waters.
catholicism: The word catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, meaning universal, and is first attested as a description of the church in the early second century. The first known use of the phrase the catholic church is in a letter written around 100 CE by Ignatius of Antioch to the Smyrnaeans. In 380 Theodosius I issued the edict De fide catolica when he established the state church of the Roman Empire.

The Catholic Church teaches that its public ministry began at Pentecost, and that the pope, the bishop of Rome, is the successor of Saint Peter. Scholars differ on the origin of the office. Some hold that Peter was the first bishop of Rome; others argue that the papacy does not depend on that view. Bart D. Ehrman and Raymond E. Brown note that a structure with a single bishop and several presbyters was adopted in Rome only in the mid-2nd century.

The church follows an episcopal polity with three levels of clergy: bishops, who hold jurisdiction over a diocese or eparchy; priests; and deacons. The pope's jurisdiction is called the Holy See, which governs through the Roman Curia. The church consists of 24 autonomous churches, of which the largest is the Latin Church and the other 23 are Eastern Catholic Churches, whose differing rites reflect historical and cultural diversity rather than differences in belief.

Catholic doctrine is rooted in the Nicene Creed. The church holds that revelation has two modes of transmission, Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, authentically interpreted by the Magisterium, its teaching authority. It teaches that Christ instituted seven sacraments. The Eucharist, offered in the Mass, is seen as the source and summit of Christian life: Catholics believe that through consecration by a priest the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.

Divisions shaped the church's relations with other Christians. The Church of the East separated after the Council of Ephesus in 431 and the Oriental Orthodox Churches after the Council of Chalcedon in 451. The separation from the Eastern Orthodox churches developed gradually, in disputes especially over papal authority, and was solidified by the Fourth Crusade. The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century led to new Christian traditions and prompted the Catholic Counter‑Reformation.

Catholic social teaching, whose foundations are widely held to have been laid by Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum in 1891, stresses care for the poor and the sick. The church is the largest non-government provider of education and medical services in the world.
central-african-republic: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in the interior of Africa, bordered by Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. Much of it is a flat or rolling plateau savanna about 500 metres above sea level. Two-thirds of the country lies within the basin of the Ubangi River, a tributary of the Congo, and the remaining third within the basin of the Chari River, which flows into Lake Chad. About 36 per cent of the country is forest, with the densest forest in the south.

The name comes from the country's location in Central Africa and its republican government. During the colonial era it was called Ubangi-Shari, after the Ubangi and Chari rivers. Barthélemy Boganda, the first prime minister, favoured the name Central African Republic, reportedly because he envisioned a larger union of countries in Central Africa. From 1976 to 1979 the country was known as the Central African Empire.

The region has been inhabited since at least 8000 BCE. About 10,000 years ago desertification forced hunter-gatherer societies south into the Sahel, where some settled and began farming. Before 3000 BCE the domestication of the African oil palm improved nutrition and allowed populations to expand. The Bouar Megaliths in the west indicate an advanced level of habitation in the late Neolithic, c. 3500 to 2700 BCE, and ironwork developed in the region around 1000 BCE. The Ubangian people settled along the Ubangi River, and some Bantu people migrated from southwest Cameroon.

In the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders raided the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile slave routes, and captives were shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia and the Western Hemisphere. In the 18th century the Bandia-Nzakara Azande peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi. In the mid 19th century the Bobangi people became major slave traders. The borders were established by France, which began annexing portions to the French Congo in the late 19th century and in 1903 created the separate colony of Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa.

The Central African Republic became independent from France in 1960. Its capital and largest city is Bangui, on the southern border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its people belong to about 80 ethnic groups, the largest being the Gbaya and the Banda. French and Sango, a creole based on the Ngbandi language, are the official languages. The Aka of the south-west have a vocal tradition of contrapuntal polyphony in four voices.
central-america: Central America is a subregion of North America, a tapering isthmus running from the southern extent of Mexico to the northwestern portion of South America. It has the Gulf of Mexico to the north, the Caribbean Sea to the northeast and the Pacific Ocean to the southwest. It is usually defined as consisting of seven countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama. The term is defined differently in different contexts. In Spanish-speaking countries the Americas are considered a single continent, América, of which Central America is a subregion.

The region has over 70 active volcanoes, and several active geological faults and the Central America Volcanic Arc make seismic activity high. The longest of its many mountain ranges are the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, the Cordillera Isabelia and the Cordillera de Talamanca. At 4,220 metres, Volcán Tajumulco is the highest peak.

Central America was formed more than 3 million years ago as part of the Isthmus of Panama. In the pre-Columbian era the northern areas were inhabited by the indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, most notably the Maya, who built numerous cities. The cultures of eastern Honduras, Caribbean Nicaragua, most of Costa Rica and Panama were predominantly speakers of Chibchan languages at the time of European contact, and are grouped by some in the Isthmo-Colombian cultural area.

Spain began its colonisation from 1502 onward. Pedro de Alvarado began the conquest of Maya territory in 1523, arriving in Soconusco, and his forces systematically conquered most of the major Maya kingdoms, including the K'iche', Tz'utujil, Pipil and Kaqchikel. By 1528 the conquest of Guatemala was nearly complete. The last independent Maya kingdoms, the Kowoj and the Itza, were defeated in 1697. In 1609 the area became the Captaincy General of Guatemala, which encompassed most of Central America except present-day Belize and Panama.

On 24 August 1821 the Spanish viceroy Juan de O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, which established the independence of New Spain. In 1838 Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua became the first of the region's states to become independent countries after the dissolution of the Federal Republic of Central America, followed by El Salvador in 1841, Panama in 1903 and Belize in 1981.

Despite the dissolution of the federation, its former members preserved a Central American identity. In Spanish, Centroamérica refers to the former members of the federation, emphasising their shared culture and history, while América Central refers to the geographical area of the seven countries between Mexico and Colombia.
chad: Chad is a landlocked country of 1,284,000 square kilometres, bordered by Libya, Sudan, Niger, Nigeria, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Its capital is 1,060 kilometres from the nearest seaport, Douala in Cameroon, and the distance and desert climate have led to the nickname Dead Heart of Africa. A wide basin is bounded by the Ennedi Plateau and the Tibesti Mountains, which include the dormant volcano Emi Koussi, at 3,414 metres. Lake Chad is the remains of an immense lake of 330,000 square kilometres that existed 7,000 years ago. The Sahara covers the northern third, a Sahelian belt lies in the centre, and savanna in the south.

From the 7th millennium BCE ecological conditions favoured settlement in the north, and some of Africa's most important archaeological sites are in the Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti Region. The earliest civilisation of the Chad Basin was the Sao, known from artefacts and oral histories, which fell to the Kanem Empire. Kanem became the first and longest-lasting of the states in the Sahelian strip, its power based on the trans-Saharan trade routes. Islamisation increased from the 11th century, and by the 12th century its scribes had developed an original script style, the barnāwī.

Kanem's expansion peaked under Mai Dunama Dabbalemi, who reigned c. 1221 to 1259. Around 1396 Bulala invaders forced Mai Umar Idrismi to move the imperial centre to Bornu. The Sultanate of Bagirmi and the Wadai Sultanate arose in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Wadai's Muhammad Sharif, who reigned from 1843 to 1858, subjugated Bagirmi and resisted French colonisation. The Territoire Militaire des Pays et Protectorats du Tchad was created in 1900, and by 1920 France had secured full control and made Chad part of French Equatorial Africa.

Chad became independent in 1960 under François Tombalbaye. Resentment of his policies in the Muslim north led to a civil war that began in 1965, and rebels took the capital in 1979. Hissène Habré defeated rival commanders, and a Chadian–Libyan conflict that began in 1978 ended in 1987 with French military intervention. Idriss Déby overthrew Habré in 1990. Chad has over 200 ethnic and linguistic groups, and its official languages are French and Arabic. Islam is practised by 55.1 per cent and Christianity by 41.1 per cent.
chagatai-khan: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
charles-darwin: Charles Robert Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at The Mount, his family's home in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, the fifth of six children of the wealthy doctor and financier Robert Darwin and Susannah Darwin, née Wedgwood. His grandfathers Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood were both prominent abolitionists, and Erasmus had praised general concepts of evolution and common descent in his Zoonomia (1794). His mother died in July 1817. In October 1825 he entered the University of Edinburgh Medical School, found lectures dull and surgery distressing, and neglected his studies. He assisted Robert Edmond Grant's research on marine invertebrates, then studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, from 1828 to 1831.

His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, established him as an eminent geologist, and his observations supported Charles Lyell's concept of gradual geological change. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) made him a popular author. Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838, but he needed time for extensive research and his geological work had priority.

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay outlining the same idea, which led to a joint submission to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, and later The Descent of Man (1871), on human evolution and sexual selection. His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881). He and his wife and cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children, two of whom died in infancy.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. By the 1870s the scientific community and most of the educated public accepted evolution as a fact, though many favoured explanations that gave natural selection only a minor role. A broad consensus that natural selection is the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s. Later movements, among them eugenics and Social Darwinism, invoked his name, sometimes against his own comments; he insisted that social policy should not be guided simply by concepts of struggle and selection.
charles-de-gaulle: Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle was born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, the third of five children. He was raised in a devoutly Roman Catholic, conservative and monarchist family. His father, Henri de Gaulle, was a professor of history and literature at a Jesuit college and later founded his own school.

In 1909 he won a place at the military academy of Saint-Cyr, finishing 119th out of 221. Before entering he served a year in the ranks in the 33rd Infantry Regiment at Arras. His company commander declined to make him a sergeant at first, remarking that the young man evidently thought nothing less than Constable of France good enough for him.

In the First World War he was wounded in the knee at the Battle of Dinant on 15 August 1914 and later taken prisoner by the German Empire. After the armistice he served on the French military mission to Poland and won the Polish Virtuti Militari. In the interwar years he advocated mobile armoured divisions.

When the German invasion came in May 1940 he led an armoured division in a counterattack and was appointed Undersecretary for War. Refusing his government's armistice with Germany, he went to Britain and urged the French to fight on in his Appeal of 18 June. He led the Free French Forces and in June 1944 became head of the Provisional Government of the French Republic. He resigned in 1946 and withdrew to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises to write his War Memoirs.

During the May 1958 crisis, as the Algerian War threatened the Fourth Republic, the National Assembly brought him back to power. He commissioned a new constitution and was elected President of France on 21 December 1958. He withdrew France from NATO's integrated military command and launched an independent nuclear force, and on 22 January 1963 he signed the Élysée Treaty with Chancellor Konrad Adenauer. He resigned in late April 1969 after losing a referendum on decentralisation.

De Gaulle died suddenly on 9 November 1970 from an abdominal aortic aneurysm while watching television. His successor Georges Pompidou announced his death by saying simply, "General de Gaulle is dead. France is a widow." French political parties and leaders claim a Gaullist legacy, and streets and monuments in France and elsewhere bear his name.
charles-dickens: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born on 7 February 1812 at Landport in Portsea Island (Portsmouth), the second of eight children of Elizabeth and John Dickens, a clerk in the Royal Navy Pay Office. He spent his formative years at Chatham in Kent, reading widely, including Tobias Smollett, Henry Fielding and The Arabian Nights. At 12 he left school to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, and after three years he returned to school.

Dickens began as a political journalist, reporting Parliamentary debates and election campaigns. His journalism in periodicals formed Sketches by Boz in 1836, Boz being a family nickname. His literary success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and within a few years he was an international celebrity. In December 1845 he became editor of the Daily News but resigned after ten weeks.

On 9 June 1865, returning from Paris with Ellen Ternan, he was in the Staplehurst rail crash in Kent, in which ten passengers were killed. He tended the wounded until rescuers came and went back for the manuscript of Our Mutual Friend.

Dickens wrote 15 major novels, several novellas and many short stories. Most were published in weekly or monthly instalments, which became the dominant Victorian mode, and let him judge his audience's reaction and sometimes change his plot. Among his works are A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849 to 1850) and Bleak House (1852 to 1853), a satire on the judicial system that helped support a reformist movement leading to the legal reform of the 1870s. His works have never gone out of print.
chavundaraya: In his own writing Chavundaraya claims descent from the Brahmakshatriya line, Brahmins who had taken Kshatriya status. The 10th-century Algodu and Arani inscriptions name him as the grandson of Govindamayya and the son of Mabalayya, a subordinate of King Marasimha II; the family's political position under that king is believed to have led to its gradual adoption of Kshatriya status. He was a devotee of the Jain teachers Nemichandra and Ajitasena Bhattaraka, and a eulogy of him is inscribed on the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar at Shravanabelagola, whose base shows him with his guru Nemichandra.

The Western Gangas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and as their commander Chavundaraya fought many battles for those overlords, beginning in the days of the Rashtrakuta king Khottiga Amoghavarsha. In the last years of Rashtrakuta rule the Gangas were threatened by civil war and by invasions of the Chola dynasty. When civil war broke out in 975 he supported Prince Rachamalla IV and installed him on the throne.

In the same year he suppressed a rebellion by Panchaldeva Mahasamanta, and in the battle of Bageyur he killed Mudurachayya, avenging the death of his own brother Nagavarma. His exploits earned him titles such as Samara Parashurama and Vira Martanda. He remained influential into the reign of Rachamalla V, who ruled from 986 to 999.

The Chavundaraya Purana, also known as the Trishashtishalaka Mahapurana, is the second oldest existing prose work in Kannada. It is based on two Sanskrit works, the Adipurana of Jinasena and the Uttarapurana of Gunabhadra, and tells the legends of sixty-three figures of Jain tradition: twenty-four tirthankaras, twelve chakravartis, nine balabhadras, nine narayanas and nine pratinarayanas. It was meant mainly for ordinary readers and avoided the complicated elements of Jain doctrine. He also wrote the Charitrasara in Sanskrit, and he patronised the Kannada grammarians Gunavarma and Nagavarma I and the poet Ranna.

The statue of Bahubali that he commissioned stands on the Indragiri hill, also called Vindhyagiri. Carved from fine-grained white granite, it is 60 feet tall, with a face measuring 6.5 feet, and has no support up to the thighs. The Chavundaraya basadi on the Chandragiri hill is credited to him by some scholars and to his son Jinadevana by others; another view holds that it was consecrated in the 11th century in his memory.
che-guevara: Ernesto Guevara was born on 14 May 1928 in Rosario, Argentina, the eldest of five children of Ernesto Guevara Lynch and Celia de la Serna y Llosa, in an upper-class family of Spanish, Basque and Irish ancestry. The family had leftist leanings. As a medical student Guevara travelled through South America and was appalled by the poverty, hunger and disease he saw.

After completing his medical degree he set out on 7 July 1953 through Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras and El Salvador. In December he arrived in Guatemala, where President Jacobo Árbenz headed a democratically elected government attempting to end the latifundia system. Árbenz's overthrow, assisted by the CIA at the behest of the United Fruit Company, solidified Guevara's political ideology.

In Mexico City Guevara met Raúl and Fidel Castro and joined the 26th of July Movement. They sailed for Cuba aboard the Granma on 25 November 1956. Batista's military attacked soon after landing, and many of the 82 men were killed or executed on capture; only 22 found each other afterwards. Guevara, who had put down his medical supplies to pick up a box of ammunition, rose to second-in-command in the two-year guerrilla campaign that deposed Fulgencio Batista.

After the revolution he reviewed appeals and death sentences of those convicted as war criminals in the revolutionary tribunals, a procedure the Cuban Ministry of Justice said most of the population supported and likened to the Nuremberg trials. He instituted agrarian land reform as minister of industries, served as president of the National Bank and travelled as a diplomat. Critics point to half-completed or empty factories left from his short tenure as minister of industries, and to the internment of people labelled anti-social in labour camps between 1965 and 1968 under the ideal of the socialist new man.

In late 1966 he went to Bolivia. He arrived in La Paz on 3 November under the false name Adolfo Mena González. His first base camp was in the remote Ñancahuazú region, where training proved hazardous and little was accomplished in building an army.

Guevara was killed in Bolivia on 9 October 1967. According to the account of his last minutes, he told the soldier guarding him that he was thinking about the immortality of the revolution, and Sergeant Terán shot him. He remains a revered and reviled figure. Admirers see a martyr and an icon of leftist movements; critics accuse him of promoting authoritarianism and endorsing violence against opponents. A photograph of him by Alberto Korda, Guerrillero Heroico, was cited by the Maryland Institute College of Art as the most widely known in the world.
china: China covers 9.6 million square kilometres, the third largest country by area, with a dry and mountainous west and both mountains and wide river valleys in the east. Chinese civilization was traditionally centred in the lowlands around the two longest rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, both of which originate on the Tibetan Plateau. Mount Everest, the world's highest point, lies on the border with Nepal. The climate is dominated by dry seasons and wet monsoons, and the Yellow River's perennial floods have devastated the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.

Modern Homo sapiens are attested in China from around 50,000 years ago, and pottery-making Neolithic cultures emerged after about 8,000 BCE. After 2000 BCE the Erlitou culture emerged in the Central Plain, controversially identified with the Xia, the traditionally accepted first dynasty; no written records confirm this. The Shang dynasty purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, and its late phase is attested by oracle bone script, the earliest known writing in China. The Zhou overthrew the Shang c. 1046 BCE, and centralised authority collapsed in 771 BCE. The Eastern Zhou saw the Spring and Autumn period and then the seven Warring States, and schools of thought such as Confucianism and Daoism.

In 221 BCE the Qin ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor, but the dynasty lasted only fifteen years. It was followed by the Han dynasty, and two millennia of imperial rule across periods of unity and division followed. The empire was succeeded by the Republic of China after the 1911 Revolution. The Warlord Era and the Chinese Civil War followed, interrupted by the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan; both sides still claim political legitimacy. The party's attempts to advance its political program faltered through famine and political turmoil, and the reform and opening-up that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy.

The 2020 census recorded a population of 1,411,778,724, and Beijing is the capital. China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party. It maintained a one-child policy from 1979 to 2015.

The Han are the dominant ethnicity, and 55 minorities are recognised, including the Hui, Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Zhuang. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chisinau: Chișinău stands on the river Bâc, a tributary of the Dniester, in the middle of Moldova, on a relatively level landscape with very fertile ground. It is roughly equidistant between the borders with Romania, 58 km away, and Ukraine, 54 km away, and very close to the geographic centre of the country. The city proper covers 120 km2 and the municipality 635 km2. Its climate is humid continental, with hot summers and cold, windy winters.

The origin of the name is unclear. One theory derives it from the archaic Romanian chișla, meaning spring or source of water, and nouă, new, because the town grew around a small spring. Another, attributed to the historian Ștefan Ciobanu, holds that it was formed like the name of Chișineu in western Romania, from the Hungarian kis, small, and Jenő, one of the seven Hungarian tribes. A third, by the linguist Kiss Lajos, derives it from a Cuman word for a grave or kurgan.

Chișinău was founded in 1436 as a monastery village and belonged to the Principality of Moldavia, which from the 16th century was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire while retaining its autonomy. At the beginning of the 19th century it was a small town of 7,000 inhabitants. In 1812, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1806-1812, the Ottomans ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to the Russian Empire. The new territory became known as Bessarabia, and Chișinău became the capital of its oblast.

A generous development plan gave the city broad, long roads by 1834 and divided it roughly into an old part with irregular buildings and a newer centre and station. Between 1830 and 1836 the architect Avraam Melnikov built the Nativity Cathedral with a bell tower, and in 1840 the Triumphal Arch, planned by Luca Zaushkevich, was completed. The belfry was demolished in Soviet times and rebuilt in 1997. After the Russian Empire the city belonged to the Moldavian Democratic Republic in 1917-1918, to the Kingdom of Romania in 1918-1940 and 1941-1944, and to the Soviet Union in 1940-1941 and 1944-1991.

Chișinău has been the capital of Moldova since 1991. It is the country's main industrial and commercial centre and its largest transport hub, and the municipality holds nearly a third of the population. The city was significantly damaged in the Second World War and by earthquakes. The architect Alexander Bernardazzi designed many buildings, including the City Hall and the Church of Saint Theodore, and much of the city is built of limestone quarried at Cricova. The house where Alexander Pushkin lived in exile is now a museum.
christopher-columbus: Scholars agree that Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa, between 25 August and 31 October 1451; theories placing his origin in Aragon or Portugal are discounted by most of them. His father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool weaver who worked in Genoa and Savona and owned a cheese stand where the boy worked. His mother was Susanna Fontanarossa. In 1470 the family moved to Savona, where Domenico took over a tavern. Columbus wrote that he went to sea at the age of 14, and he later settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew ran a cartography workshop.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, the Silk Road was closed to Christian traders. In 1474 the Florentine astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli suggested to King Afonso V of Portugal that sailing west across the Atlantic would reach Asia faster than the route around Africa, but the king rejected the idea. Columbus and his brother proposed such a plan in the 1480s, and Bartolomeu Dias's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 complicated it. After the Granada War and years of lobbying, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II of Spain agreed to sponsor the voyage.

Columbus left the Port of Palos in August 1492 with three ships and made landfall on 12 October on an island in the Bahamas known to its inhabitants as Guanahani. He then visited Cuba and Hispaniola, where he founded the short-lived fort of La Navidad, and returned to Castile in early 1493 with captured American Indians. Three further voyages took him to the Lesser Antilles in 1493, to Trinidad and the northern coast of South America in 1498, and to the east coast of Central America in 1502. He never clearly renounced his belief that he had reached the Far East, and he called the people he met indios.

As colonial governor Columbus was accused by some contemporaries of significant brutality, and he was arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500. He afterwards demanded the tenth of the new lands' wealth promised in the Capitulations of Santa Fe, and after his death his heirs pursued the claim in the protracted lawsuits known as the pleitos colombinos. His remains were moved several times, between Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo and perhaps Havana, and DNA tests on those in Seville in 2003 led researchers to conclude that they are his.

His voyages began lasting contact between the two hemispheres and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, diseases and ideas. Diseases and warfare introduced from the Old World contributed to the decline of Hispaniola's American Indians, who were also enslaved and mistreated under Columbus's government. Once idealized as a heroic discoverer, he is now examined more critically.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BCE in Arpinum, a hill town 100 kilometres south-east of Rome, into a wealthy family of the equestrian order. His father was in poor health and could not enter public life, so he studied extensively to compensate. The cognomen Cicero comes from the Latin for chickpea, cicer. Plutarch explains that it was first given to an ancestor with a cleft in the tip of his nose resembling a chickpea, and says that Cicero refused to change the name when he entered politics.

His first major appearance in the courts came in 81 BCE, at 26. In 80 BCE he defended Sextus Roscius of Ameria on a charge of parricide in Pro Roscio Amerino, his first criminal case. He accused Chrysogonus, a freedman of the dictator Sulla, of fabricating the proscription of Roscius's father to obtain the family's property, while tactfully avoiding any charge against Sulla himself. He won and gained a good reputation as an orator.

Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE with the support of every unit of the centuriate assembly. He suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy, but because he had executed five of the conspirators without trial he was exiled in 58 BCE and recalled the next year. In 60 BCE he refused Julius Caesar's invitation to join the partnership of Caesar, Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus, fearing it would undermine the Republic.

In 51 BCE he reluctantly took the proconsulship of Cilicia, where he restored calm by mild government and recovered public property embezzled by previous governors. In Caesar's civil war he favoured Pompey and followed the Pompeian forces to Pharsalus, but after Caesar's victory there on 9 August 48 BCE he refused to take command and returned to Rome in 47 BCE.

After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE Cicero opposed Mark Antony in a series of speeches called the Philippics, and he praised Caesar's heir Octavian to play him against Antony. When Octavian and Antony joined with Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was proscribed and executed in late 43 BCE, on 7 December, while trying to escape Italy. On Antony's order his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra.

Cicero is considered the master of Latin prose. He coined much of Latin's philosophical vocabulary. Of his speeches 88 were recorded and 52 survive. Petrarch's rediscovery of his letters is often credited with starting the 14th-century Renaissance, and his authority peaked in the 18th-century Enlightenment.
cold-war: Animosity between the Allies of the Second World War predated its end. After the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt in April 1945, the administration of Harry Truman took a harder line, and diplomats disputed how to read the Yalta agreements, the composition of the Polish government and the running of the United Nations. In February 1946 George F. Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow helped shape American strategy, and on 5 March Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton. The term itself was used by George Orwell in 1945 and applied to the confrontation by Bernard Baruch on 16 April 1947.

The United States declared the Truman Doctrine of containment in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan in 1948 and founded NATO in 1949; the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact followed in 1955. Early confrontations were the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, which ended in a stalemate. The Soviet Union tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949. After Joseph Stalin died in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev denounced him in 1956, the year the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian Revolution. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely considered the closest the war came to nuclear conflict.

Both powers courted the newly decolonised states, and the Vietnam War of 1955 to 1975 ended in a North Vietnamese victory. In Indonesia from 1965 to 1966 the military, with the aid of the United States and other Western governments, led the mass killing of more than 500,000 members and sympathisers of the Indonesian Communist Party. The Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia with the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and a period of détente in the 1970s brought treaties limiting nuclear arsenals. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 renewed tensions.

Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985. In June 1987 he announced perestroika, an agenda of economic restructuring, and introduced glasnost, or openness. These reforms contributed to the revolutions of 1989 in the Eastern Bloc and to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, which ended the Cold War.

By 1989 the United States had military alliances with 50 countries and 526,000 troops stationed abroad. Nearly 100,000 Americans died in the Korean and Vietnam Wars, and millions died in the proxy wars around the globe, most of all in eastern Asia. Historians have disagreed over who was responsible for the breakdown of relations: orthodox accounts blame the Soviet Union, revisionists place more responsibility on the United States, and post-revisionists see a more nuanced pattern.
colorado: Colorado is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. It shares the Four Corners region with Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is bordered by Wyoming to the north, Nebraska to the northeast, Kansas to the east and Oklahoma to the southeast. It takes in most of the Southern Rocky Mountains, the northeastern portion of the Colorado Plateau and the western edge of the Great Plains, and its landscape includes alpine mountains, high plains, deserts with huge sand dunes and deep canyons.

In 1861 the United States Congress defined the boundaries of the new Territory of Colorado exclusively by lines of latitude and longitude, from 37°N to 41°N and from 102°02′48″W to 109°02′48″W. After 165 years of government surveys the borders were officially defined by 697 boundary markers and 697 straight lines. Colorado, Wyoming and Utah are the only states whose borders are defined solely by straight lines with no natural features. The Four Corners Monument is the only place in the United States where four states meet.

The region has been inhabited by Native Americans and their Paleo-Indian ancestors for at least 13,500 years and possibly more than 37,000. The Lindenmeier site contains artifacts dating from approximately 8720 BCE. The Ancient Pueblo peoples lived in the valleys and mesas of the Colorado Plateau in the far southwest, and the Ute Nation inhabited the mountain valleys of the Rocky Mountains. The Apache and Comanche lived in the east and southeast. In the 17th century the Arapaho and Cheyenne moved west from the Great Lakes region to hunt across the High Plains.

The United States acquired the territorial claim to the eastern Rocky Mountains with the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803. In 1806 Zebulon Pike led an army reconnaissance expedition into the disputed region. Spanish cavalry arrested him and his troops in the San Luis Valley the following February, took them to Chihuahua and expelled them from Mexico in July.

In 1848 much of the Nuevo México region was annexed to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The Pike's Peak Gold Rush of 1858-1862 brought an influx of settlers. On 28 February 1861 President James Buchanan signed the act creating the Territory of Colorado, and on 1 August 1876 President Ulysses S. Grant signed Proclamation 230, admitting Colorado as the 38th state.

Denver is the capital, the most populous city and the centre of the Front Range Urban Corridor. Colorado Springs is the second-most populous city. The state is the eighth-largest by area. Its economy rests on government and defense, mining, agriculture, tourism and manufacturing.
concepcion-chile: Concepción was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1550 north of the Bío Bío River, at the site now known as Penco. It was named Concepción de María Purísima del Nuevo Extremo. The settlement lay a few kilometres north of La Frontera, the boundary between Spanish territory and the land of the Mapuche, who remained independent until the 1870s. Spanish authorities formally recognised it as a town two years later by royal decree and gave it a coat of arms still in use today. When the Spanish arrived, the chronicler Jerónimo de Vivar noted that local Mapuche wore gold and silver bracelets and crown-like ornaments, interpreted either as Incan gifts, war spoils or the adoption of Incan metallurgy.

The city was the capital of the Kingdom of Chile between 1565 and 1573 and kept the unofficial position of military capital for the rest of the colonial period. After a serious earthquake in 1751 it moved to the Valle de la Mocha, where the city centre and historic district now stand. Its inhabitants are still called penquistas, after Penco. The city was an important site in the struggle for Chile's independence, and the declaration of independence was held at the Plaza de la Independencia. Until the election of Manuel Montt as president in 1851, executive power in independent Chile was dominated by Concepción elites.

Concepción is the capital of the Biobío Region and of Concepción Province, about 500 km south of Santiago. It is the core of the Greater Concepción metropolitan area, the second largest city in Chile by urban area, and sits in the most heavily industrialized region of the country. It is known as the university city, with the Universidad de Concepción, the Universidad del Biobío and the Catholic University of the Most Holy Conception. Like most of Chile it is seismically active: an earthquake in 1939 destroyed much of the city, one in 1953 damaged 15 per cent of its buildings, and a major earthquake in 1960 had a nearby epicentre.
confucius: The name Confucius is a Latinized form of the Mandarin Kǒngfūzǐ, meaning roughly Great Master Kong, coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu, meaning hill or mound. His courtesy name was Zhongni, the Zhong indicating that he was the second son in his family.

It is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was formally controlled by the kings of Zhou but effectively independent under the local lords of Lu. His father Kong He, an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison, died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty.

Traditional accounts trace the family back through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty, though not all modern scholars accept this descent. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi, and a year later their son Kong Li was born. He is said to have held various government jobs in his early 20s and to have mourned his mother for three years.

In the Analects, Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who invented nothing. He put the most emphasis on study and wanted his disciples to master older classics rather than build a systematic theory.
