Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing particular assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy associated with him are more ancient, and the Analects were compiled many years after his death. His ethics stress self-cultivation and emulation of moral exemplars over rules, and he taught a negative form of the Golden Rule, sometimes called the Silver Rule.

His disciples and his grandson Zisi continued his school, and Mencius in the 4th century BCE and Xunzi in the 3rd century BCE elaborated his ideas in different ways. The Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted Legalism as its official doctrine. Under Emperor Wu of Han, works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy and required reading for civil service examinations in 140 BCE, a practice continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912.
connecticut: Connecticut is bordered by Long Island Sound to the south, New York to the west, Massachusetts to the north and Rhode Island to the east. It is named after the Connecticut River, the longest in New England, which roughly bisects the state. The river's name derives from anglicized spellings of Quinnetuket, a Mohegan-Pequot word for long tidal river. Many coastal towns lie less than 20 feet above sea level, and because the coast is on Long Island Sound, an estuary, it is relatively protected from high storm waves.

Evidence of human presence dates back 10,000 years. The peoples were semi-nomadic and shared Algonquian languages. In the early 17th century about 8,000 Pequots lived in the south-east, a number roughly halved by the smallpox epidemic of 1633–34, and 1,500 to 2,500 Mohegans lived west of the Thames. Their economies combined hunting, shellfishing, gathering and maize agriculture, and wampum from quahog and whelk shells served as currency and as a record of agreements.

In 1633 the Dutch West India Company established a short-lived settlement, House of Hope, in Hartford. The Dutch colony of New Netherland initially claimed half of Connecticut, but the English founded the first major settlements at about the same time. Thomas Hooker led followers from the Massachusetts Bay Colony to form the Connecticut Colony, and the Saybrook and New Haven Colonies, founded by other settlers from Massachusetts, had both merged into it by the mid-1660s. The Fundamental Orders of 1638–39 framed its first government, and King Charles II granted a charter in 1662.

Connecticut was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rejected British rule. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Connecticut Compromise, a bicameral Congress with proportional representation in the House and equal representation of the states in the Senate. In January 1788 Connecticut became the fifth state to ratify the Constitution. Hartford became the sole capital in 1875; before then New Haven and Hartford alternated.

Hartford is the capital and Bridgeport the most populous city. Connecticut is the third-smallest state by area. Its nickname, the Constitution State, was adopted in 1959. Yale University stands in New Haven, and the United States Coast Guard Academy in New London.
copenhagen: Copenhagen lies on the eastern shore of the island of Zealand, partly on the island of Amager and on a number of natural and artificial islets between the two. It faces the Øresund, the strait that separates Denmark from Sweden and connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea. The Swedish city of Malmö lies directly across the sound, 42 kilometres away by road.

The Danish name København reflects the city's origin as a harbour and a place of commerce. The Old Norse form was Kaupmannahǫfn, meaning 'merchants' harbour', and the present form developed through sound changes that took place around 1400. The Latin name Hafnia is the source of the name of the element hafnium.

Flint tools show settlement in the Stone Age, and many historians believe the town dates to the late Viking Age, possibly founded by Sweyn I Forkbeard. The first habitations were probably centred on Gammel Strand, 'old shore'. The natural harbour and good herring stocks attracted seasonal fishermen and merchants from the 11th century and more permanent residents in the 13th. Excavations have uncovered the remains of a large merchant mansion from about 1020 near Kongens Nytorv, and a well from the late 12th century in Pilestræde.

Copenhagen became the capital of Denmark in the early 15th century, and the University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479. In the 16th century it served as the de facto capital of the Kalmar Union and its monarchy, and by the 17th century it was the centre of the Danish government and military. The 18th century brought a devastating plague outbreak and urban fires, followed by the building of the district of Frederiksstaden and of institutions such as the Royal Theatre and the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. In this period the city was the centre of the Danish slave trade.

A British fleet bombarded the city in 1807 during the Napoleonic Wars. The Danish Golden Age that followed gave Copenhagen a neoclassical look. After the Second World War the Finger Plan guided the growth of housing and businesses along five urban railway routes running out from the centre.

Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark and its cultural, economic and governmental centre. Since the completion of the Øresund Bridge it has been increasingly integrated with Malmö and the Swedish province of Scania in the Øresund Region. Its landmarks include Tivoli Gardens, the Amalienborg and Christiansborg palaces, Rosenborg Castle and Frederik's Church, and the University of Copenhagen is the oldest university in Denmark.
copper: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu, from the Latin cuprum, and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, second only to silver among pure metals at room temperature. Pure copper is orange-red, one of the few metals with a natural colour other than grey or silver. In air it slowly forms a protective layer of copper oxide, and on old roofs and the Statue of Liberty a green layer of verdigris appears. Copper is also one of the few native metals, found in nature in a directly usable, unalloyed form.

The use of native copper dates to about 9000 BCE in the Middle East, and a native copper pendant found in northern Iraq dates to 8700 BCE. The history of copper metallurgy is thought to run from cold working of native copper to annealing, then smelting, and finally casting. The earliest archaeological evidence of hot metallurgy in Eurasia, in the Balkans and Carpathian Mountains, dates to between 6200 and 5000 BCE. An amulet from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, dated to 4000 BCE, is the earliest example of lost-wax casting in copper. Ötzi the Iceman, who lived between 3300 and 3200 BCE, was found with a copper axehead of 99.7 per cent purity.

Smelting was probably discovered in China before 2800 BCE, in Central America around 600 CE and in West Africa about the 9th or 10th century. Experience with copper helped the development of other metals, and copper smelting likely led to the discovery of iron smelting.

Copper was alloyed with zinc to make brass and with tin to make bronze, and copper-tin bronzes have been used to make bells for centuries, the composition of the alloy affecting the tone. Alloys of copper and nickel, called cupronickel, are used in low-denomination coins. In Japan, shakudō is a decorative alloy of copper with 4 to 10 per cent gold, which can be patinated to dark blue or black. For more than two centuries copper paint has been used on boat hulls to control the growth of plants and shellfish.
crimea: Crimea covers 27,000 square kilometres on the northern coast of the Black Sea and the western coast of the Sea of Azov. It is almost an island, joined to the mainland only by the Isthmus of Perekop, a strip about 5 to 7 kilometres wide. It was called the Tauric Peninsula, after the Tauri, until the early modern period; the name Crimea comes from the Italian la Crimea. Most of the peninsula is semiarid steppe, scattered with the burial mounds of the ancient Scythians, while the Crimean Mountains shelter a narrow southern coast with a Mediterranean climate.

The recorded history of Crimea begins around the 5th century BCE, when Greek colonies were founded on the south coast, the most important being Chersonesos near modern Sevastopol, with Scythians and Tauri in the hinterland. The south later became the Bosporan Kingdom, a client kingdom of Rome from 63 BCE to 341 CE, and stayed Greek in culture under the Byzantine Empire, the Empire of Trebizond and the Principality of Theodoro, which ended in 1475. In the 13th century the Venetians and the Genoese held some ports, while the interior fell to the Golden Horde.

In the 1440s the Crimean Khanate formed from the collapse of the Horde and soon became subject to the Ottoman Empire, which also conquered the independent coastal areas. Raids on Eastern Europe for slaves were a major source of prosperity. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 made the Tatars of Crimea politically independent, and in 1783 Catherine the Great incorporated the peninsula into the Russian Empire. From 1853 to 1856 it was the site of the principal engagements of the Crimean War, in which Russia lost to a French-led alliance.

Crimea changed hands many times in the Russian Civil War, and Wrangel's White Army made its last stand there. In 1921 it became an autonomous republic within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Germany occupied it from 1942 to 1944, and after the Soviets regained control in 1944 they deported the Crimean Tatars and several other nationalities. It became an oblast in 1945 and was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1954, on the 300th anniversary of the Treaty of Pereyaslav.

After Ukrainian independence in 1991 most of the peninsula became the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, and a 1997 treaty let Russia keep basing its fleet in Sevastopol, the largest city. In 2014 Russia occupied and annexed the peninsula, a step most countries do not recognise. Its population is about 2.4 million.
croatia: Croatia lies on the Adriatic coast, and the sea forms its entire southwest border. It covers 56,594 square kilometres and is divided into twenty counties within four historical and cultural regions. The Dinaric Alps rise to the highest point, the Dinara peak at 1,831 metres, near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Insular Croatia consists of over a thousand islands and islets, 48 of them permanently inhabited; the largest are Cres and Krk.

In the north the hilly Hrvatsko Zagorje and the plains of Slavonia are crossed by the Danube, Drava, Kupa and Sava. Karst topography makes up about half of the country. The area around Dubrovnik is a practical exclave, separated by land from the rest by a short coastal strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linked to it by the Pelješac Bridge.

The area was inhabited throughout prehistory, and Neanderthal fossils from the middle Palaeolithic were found at Krapina. Illyrians and Liburnians lived there, and the first Greek colonies were established on the islands of Hvar, Korčula and Vis. In 9 CE the territory became part of the Roman Empire. Emperor Diocletian, a native of the region, built a large palace at Split and retired there after abdicating in 305 CE. In the 5th century Julius Nepos, the last de jure Western Roman Emperor, ruled a small realm from it after fleeing Italy in 475.

Avar and Croat invasions in the late 6th and first half of the 7th century destroyed almost all Roman towns. Survivors retreated to the coast, islands and mountains, and Dubrovnik was founded by survivors from Epidaurum. The origin of the Croats is debated: the predominant view is that the White Croats were a Slavic group who migrated during the Migration Period, while the Iranian theory proposes a Sarmatian-Alanic origin, drawing on names in the Tanais Tablets. The oldest stone inscription with the full ethnonym styles Duke Branimir as Dux Cruatorvm, probably between 879 and 892.

Croatia is a unitary constitutional republic with a parliamentary system. The president is directly elected for five years, and the Sabor, a unicameral parliament, holds legislative power. Its population was an estimated 3.87 million in 2024, down from a peak of 4.7 million in 1991. The 2021 census recorded 91.6% Croats and 3.2% Serbs, and about 4 million Croats live abroad. The country has ten sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The necktie derives from the cravat worn by 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France.
cuba: Cuba is an archipelago of 4,195 islands, cays and islets in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Gulf of Mexico meets the Atlantic Ocean. Key West, Florida, lies about 150 kilometres across the Straits of Florida to the north and northwest, Mexico 210 kilometres west across the Yucatán Channel, Haiti 78 kilometres to the east and Jamaica 148 kilometres to the south. The main island is 1,250 kilometres long and makes up most of the land area of 104,338 square kilometres. It consists mostly of flat to rolling plains apart from the Sierra Maestra in the southeast, whose highest point is Pico Turquino at 1,974 metres. The second-largest island is Isla de la Juventud.

Humans first settled Cuba around 6,000 years ago. The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno arrived from South America about 1,700 years ago and, unlike the earlier settlers, produced pottery and practised intensive agriculture. The earliest evidence of the Taíno on Cuba dates to the 9th century. Descendants of the first settlers persisted in the west of the island until European contact as the hunter-gathering Guanahatabey. Christopher Columbus first arrived on 27 October 1492, claimed the island for Spain and named it Isla Juana after John, Prince of Asturias.

The first Spanish settlement was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar at Baracoa in 1511, and San Cristóbal de la Habana was founded in 1514 and moved to its present place in 1519, becoming the capital in 1607. The Taíno were forced to work under the encomienda system.

Within a century they suffered high mortality, primarily from Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity, aggravated by harsh colonial subjugation. In 1529 a measles outbreak killed two-thirds of the few who had survived smallpox. Cuba remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898, was then occupied by the United States, and became independent in 1902. The Cuban Revolution of January 1959 overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.

Havana is the capital and largest city. Cuba is a socialist republic whose constitution names the Communist Party as the leading force of society and the state. Spanish culture, West African culture and the Guanahatabey and Taíno inheritance together shape Cuban culture. Cuba's population descends primarily from Spanish settlers, sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, and pre-Columbian peoples, chiefly the Taíno and Ciboney. Havana, Camagüey, Cienfuegos and Trinidad, with colonial centres in Baroque and Neoclassical styles, are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
cyprus: Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia. It measures 240 kilometres from end to end and 100 kilometres at its widest, and lies 75 kilometres south of Turkey. Two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, enclose the central Mesaoria plain. The highest point is Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, in the Troodos range. Some sources place the island in Europe and others in Western Asia, within the Levant.

Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, at about the time the island's pygmy hippopotamus and dwarf elephant became extinct. Neolithic farming communities emerged by around 8500 BCE, and the village of Khirokitia dates to approximately 6800 BCE.

From around 1650 BCE copper from the Troodos Mountains drove trade and the growth of urban settlements, and the island, identified in whole or part as Alashiya, was ruled by kings who corresponded with the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt, as the Amarna letters document. Mycenaean Greeks traded there from around 1400 BCE, and a major wave of Greek settlement is believed to have followed the collapse of Mycenaean Greece.

Later the island was contested by the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, and Alexander the Great seized it in 333 BCE. Ptolemaic, Roman, Arab, Lusignan and Venetian rule followed, then Ottoman dominion from 1571 to 1878. Britain administered Cyprus from 1878 under the Cyprus Convention and annexed it formally in 1914. Independence came in 1960. Intercommunal violence in 1963 and 1964 displaced more than 25,000 Turkish Cypriots into enclaves.

A coup by Greek Cypriot nationalists and elements of the Greek military junta on 15 July 1974 was followed by the Turkish invasion of 20 July, which captured the north and displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots. A Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey. The island is divided along a United Nations buffer zone, and two British sovereign military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, remain in the south.

The Republic of Cyprus, a presidential republic, joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro on 1 January 2008. Greek and Turkish Cypriots share many customs, such as the foods souvla and halloumi, but differ in religion: Greek Cypriots are traditionally Greek Orthodox and Turkish Cypriots Sunni Muslim.
czech-republic: The Czech Republic is a hilly, landlocked country of 78,871 square kilometres, bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland and Slovakia. It is traditionally divided into three lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east and Czech Silesia in the northeast. Bohemia is a basin drained by the Elbe and the Vltava, surrounded by low mountains such as the Giant Mountains, where Sněžka, at 1,603 metres, is the highest point in the country. Moravia is hilly and drained mainly by the Morava River.

Water from the country flows to three seas: the North Sea, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. The Czech Republic also leases the Moldauhafen, a lot in the Hamburg Docks awarded to Czechoslovakia by Article 363 of the Treaty of Versailles; the territory reverts to Germany in 2028.

The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, dated to approximately 29,000 to 25,000 BCE, is considered the oldest known ceramic figurine in the world. After Celtic migrations in the 3rd century BCE, Bohemia became associated with the Boii. In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first documented Slavic state in Central Europe. Great Moravia reached its zenith in the 9th century under Svatopluk I, and was Christianized with the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius, who codified Old Church Slavonic and the Glagolitic script.

The Přemyslid dynasty unified the Duchy of Bohemia in the late 9th century. In the early 13th century Přemysl Ottokar I obtained the Golden Bull of Sicily from the emperor, confirming his and his descendants' royal status, and the duchy was raised to a kingdom. German immigrants settled in the periphery in the 13th century, and the Mongols, in their invasion of Europe, were defensively defeated at Olomouc after raiding Moravia.

The Czech Republic is a pluralist parliamentary democracy with a bicameral parliament: the 200-member Chamber of Deputies and the 81-member Senate. From 1993 to 2012 the president was chosen by parliament, and since 2013 by direct election.

In the 2021 census 57.3% of inhabitants were Czechs and 3.4% Moravians. About 75% to 79% of residents declare no religion. The Jewish population of Bohemia and Moravia, 118,000 in 1930, was nearly annihilated in the Holocaust.
